proposals.before: When Suiren drilled fire, Paoxi emerged in the Zhen (east) trigram; wind took lineage and descended to Wu; blazing heirs broadened the foundation; dividing the wilds is not heard of—their return is one measure.
proposals.after: When Suiren drilled fire, Paoxi emerged in the Zhen (east) trigram; the Feng lineage descended to the martial kings, and the Yan heirs broadened the foundation; dividing the wilds is not heard of—their return is one measure.
proposals.reason: 風宗下武 and 炎胤昌基 name ancestral Feng and Yan lines, not wind taking lineage and descending to a person Wu; the current literal English is unintelligible.

proposals.before: The Han geography adds that Gaozu created twenty-six units and that Emperor Wu renamed the three inner belts Jingzhao, Fengyi, and Fufeng—the region later called the Three Adjuncts of Chang'an.〉
proposals.after: The Treatise on Geography says: Gaozu added twenty-six; Emperor Wu changed Heshang, Weinan, and Zhongdi into Jingzhao, Fengyi, and Fufeng—these are the Three Adjuncts.〉
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English invents Chang'an, turns 地理志曰 into a vague 'Han geography adds', and omits the three pre-rename districts named in the Chinese.

proposals.before: Yong became Liang, Liang became Yi, Xuzhou returned to the rolls, southern Jiaozhi and northern Shuofang were wired in, and the old Xia-style names were revived until the realm sat in thirteen inspectorates.
proposals.after: Yong was changed to Liang, Liang to Yi; Xuzhou was further established; Xia's old designations were restored; Jiaozhi was set up in the south and Shuofang in the north—thirteen departments in all.
proposals.reason: 'Wired in' is unidiomatic and obscures 南置交阯，北有朔方; the Chinese is a list of administrative changes totaling thirteen departments.

proposals.before: Under Emperors He and Shun the map was redrawn nine times.
proposals.after: Under Emperors He and Shun names were altered; there were nine of them.
proposals.reason: 其名有九 means nine names (as the following note lists), not nine successive redrawings of the map.

proposals.before: When Cao Cao seized the north the realm split three ways, the people were scattered like tablets on a flood, the old capitals lay in ruins, and he could found only twelve new commanderies,
proposals.after: When Wei Wu settled his hegemony, the three sides stood like a tripod, the people were thrown into turmoil, the passes and Luo region lay desolate, and those he established were twelve,
proposals.reason: 版蕩 is the set phrase for political turmoil, not tablets on a flood; 關洛 means the passes and the Luo region, not a generic 'old capitals'; 魏武 is a title, rendered only as Cao Cao.

proposals.before: 〈from Xinxing down the Han river arc to Xiangyang, twelve seats in all.〉
proposals.after: 〈Xinxing, Leping, Xiping, Xinping, Lueyang, Yinping, Daifang, Qiao, Leling, Zhangwu, Nanxiang, and Xiangyang.〉
proposals.reason: The Chinese note is a plain list of twelve commandery names; the idiomatic version invents a Han-river arc and an explicit count not present in this unit.

proposals.before: Everyone nods when you name the Luo shoals or Xianyang as the heart of Qin and Han, or liken Jin's hold on the western riverbank to the world Yao and Shun knew; every schoolchild can chant how the new capital sits where Haojing once stood—truths so worn smooth by memory that the official annals pass them by in silence.
proposals.after: Everyone nods when you name the Luo shoals or Xianyang as the heart of Qin and Han, or liken Jin's hold on the western riverbank to the world Yao and Yu knew; every schoolchild can chant how the new capital sits where Haojing once stood—truths so worn smooth by memory that the official annals pass them by in silence.
proposals.reason: Chinese 堯禹 is Yao and Yu; the idiomatic English substitutes Shun (舜) for Yu (禹).

proposals.before: Legend places Fuxi's birth at Chenji and his enthronement at Chen.
proposals.after: Legend places Fuxi's birth at Chenji; he became Son of Heaven and made his capital at Chen.
proposals.reason: Chinese 而爲天子，都於陳 means he became Son of Heaven and established the capital at Chen, not that he was enthroned at Chen.

proposals.before: When Emperor Hui fell to calamity the Central Plain was lost; after the Yongjia flight south the court set its capital at Jiankang by imperial decree, holding barely two shares of a realm once counted in ninths.
proposals.after: When Emperor Hui fell to calamity the Central Plain was lost; after the Yongjia flight south the court set its capital at Jianye by imperial decree, holding barely two shares of a realm once counted in ninths.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names 建鄴 (Jianye); Jiankang is a later name of the same city not used in this unit.

proposals.before: Some clans took names from ancestral seats, others earned fiefs for deeds done—and the old domains of Qi, You, Yan, and Qi all fall inside these bounds.
proposals.after: Some clans took names from ancestral seats, others earned fiefs for deeds done—and the old domains of Qi (祁), You, Yan, and Qi (齊) all fall inside these bounds.
proposals.reason: The first item is 祁, not the state 齊; rendering both as undifferentiated Qi collapses two names.

proposals.before: Each provincial lord knelt to one of the king's two senior regents, splitting the world into eastern and western halves—the Two Chiefs of high Zhou.
proposals.after: Each provincial lord attached with his dependents to two elders of the Son of Heaven; they divided the realm into left and right, called the two bo.
proposals.reason: The Chinese 曰二伯 does not name Zhou; 'high Zhou' is an invented gloss.

proposals.before: Those ladders raised campaigns, drafted ditch gangs, mustered night watchmen, and split the grain and corvée rolls.
proposals.after: By this they raised armies, performed field labor and corvée, compared pursuit and night patrol, and ordered tribute and taxes.
proposals.reason: Chinese 以起軍旅 continues the Zhouli functions; 'Those ladders' is an invented subject not present in the source.

proposals.before: Wayfarers found a lodge every ten li with water and a warm bowl.
proposals.after: The supply officer: every ten li there was a hut, and the hut had drink and food.
proposals.reason: 遺人 is the Zhouli supply-officer office heading this regulation, not anonymous wayfarers.

proposals.before: From the Wen-Jing recovery to the second year of Yuansheng under Emperor Ping, the census recorded 12,233,062 households and 59,594,978 persons on a domain stretching 9,302 li east-west and 13,368 li north-south.
proposals.after: From the Wen-Jing recovery to the second year of Yuanshi under Emperor Ping, the census recorded 12,233,062 households and 59,594,978 persons on a domain stretching 9,302 li east-west and 13,368 li north-south.
proposals.reason: The source era name is 元始 (Yuanshi), not Yuansheng.

proposals.before: Emperor Xian Jian'an first year enfeoffed Cao Cao as General Who Stabilizes the East, enfeoffed Feiting precinct marquis.
proposals.after: Emperor Xian Jian'an first year appointed Cao Cao General Who Stabilizes the East, and enfeoffed him as Feiting precinct marquis.
proposals.reason: The verb 拜 marks appointment to 鎮東將軍; only 封費亭侯 is an enfeoffment.

proposals.before: In Huangchu 3 Cao Pi decreed that a king's younger sons became township dukes, an heir-apparent king's younger sons precinct marquises,[4] and younger sons of dukes and marquises precinct earls.
proposals.after: In Huangchu 3 Cao Pi decreed that a king's sons by secondary consorts became township dukes, an heir-apparent king's sons by secondary consorts precinct marquises,[4] and sons by secondary consorts of dukes and marquises precinct earls.
proposals.reason: 庶子 means sons of secondary consorts, not younger sons.

proposals.before: Southern principalities had kept a third of their rent for the throne, but after Yuandi crossed the Yangzi the court in Taixing 1 cut the royal share to one-ninth.
proposals.after: The various states east of the Jiang had all drawn one-third of their revenues as food-income; after Emperor Yuan crossed the Yangzi, in the first year of Taixing the court first set that princely share at one-ninth.
proposals.reason: 三分食一 and 九分食一 state the fraction the princes themselves received, not a share reserved for the throne.

proposals.before: 〈Marquis Wu of Jin transferred his court here from Quwo.〉
proposals.after: 〈Duke Wu of Jin transferred his court here from Quwo.〉
proposals.reason: Chinese Jin Wugong is Duke Wu of Jin (gong); Marquis mismatches the source title.

proposals.before: Marquis Wu of Jin relocated his seat here from Jinyang.〉
proposals.after: Duke Wu of Jin relocated his seat here from Jinyang.〉
proposals.reason: Chinese Jin Wugong is Duke Wu of Jin (gong); Marquis mismatches the source title.

proposals.before: King Wu of Zhou granted this ground to the line of Taibo, elder uncle of the Zhou house.〉
proposals.after: King Wu of Zhou granted this ground to the posterity of Taibo of Western Zhou.〉
proposals.reason: Chinese names Taibo of Western Zhou and his descendants; elder uncle of the Zhou house is not in the source clause.

proposals.before: There is Thunder-Head Mountain; Yi and Qi dwelt on its south, the so-called Shouyang Mountain.〉
proposals.after: There is Thunder-Head Mountain; Boyi and Shuqi dwelt on its south, the so-called Shouyang Mountain.〉
proposals.reason: The pair Yi Qi is the conventional pair Boyi and Shuqi, not truncated Yi and Qi.

proposals.before: Linyu and Huojia counties.
proposals.after: Linlü and Huojia counties.
proposals.reason: 林慮 is Linlü (Linlü/Linxū), not Linyu; the idiomatic county name is a phonetic error.

proposals.before: Linyu Huojia.
proposals.after: Linlü Huojia.
proposals.reason: The literal line repeats the same wrong romanization of 林慮 as Linyu.

proposals.before: 〈Cao Cao's raid on Yuan Shao's grain depots at Wuchao unfolded southeast of here.〉
proposals.after: 〈Wuchao ground lies to the southeast.〉
proposals.reason: The Chinese only locates Wuchao ground southeast of the counties; it does not name Cao Cao, Yuan Shao, or a grain-depot raid.

proposals.before: 〈The old Kuang fort where Confucius was cornered between Chen and Cai.〉
proposals.after: 〈The old Kuang city, where Confucius was besieged.〉
proposals.reason: The Chinese says formerly Kuang city, where Confucius was in distress; it does not mention Chen or Cai.

proposals.before: 〈Heartland of the Ji polity whose lords bore the Si surname.〉
proposals.after: 〈Formerly the state of Qi (Ji).〉
proposals.reason: The Chinese is only 故杞國, formerly the Ji/Qi polity; it does not mention a Si surname or a heartland gloss.

proposals.before: 〈Preserves the Chu Mound watch post of old Qi.〉
proposals.after: 〈There is Chuchiu pavilion.〉
proposals.reason: The Chinese names only Chuchiu pavilion and does not attribute it to old Qi.

proposals.before: 〈The classic hunt where Confucius saw the unicorn took place here.〉
proposals.after: 〈The place where Lu captured the unicorn.〉
proposals.reason: The Chinese is 魯獲麟所, where Lu captured the lin; it does not name Confucius or a classic hunt.

proposals.before: 〈Therefore called Pingyang.〉
proposals.after: 〈Formerly called Pingyang.〉
proposals.reason: 故 here means formerly, not therefore; the literal line reverses that sense.

proposals.before: After Wei yielded the mandate to Cao Pi the capital shifted to Luoyang, but the Xu halls and arsenals stayed in use under the new name Xuchang.〉
proposals.after: After the abdication to Wei the capital shifted to Luoyang, but the Xu halls and arsenals stayed in use under the new name Xuchang.〉
proposals.reason: 魏禪 after 漢獻帝都許 is the Han abdication to Wei, not Wei yielding the mandate to Cao Pi.

proposals.before: Zhenyang, Bei, Yichun, Langling, and Yang'an marked the old Jiang kingdom.
proposals.after: Zhenyang, Beiyichun, Langling, and Yang'an marked the old Jiang kingdom.
proposals.reason: Chinese Beiyichun is one county name; splitting it as Bei and Yichun invents a county.

proposals.before: 〈Xuandi of Han first drew his fief from this town.〉
proposals.after: 〈Emperor Xuan first received his fief in this town.〉
proposals.reason: Chinese Xuandi at Wuyang in this Jin geography is Jin Xuandi, not Han Xuandi.

proposals.before: 〈The old Hu viscounty on the Huai marches.〉
proposals.after: 〈Formerly the state of the Hu viscount.〉
proposals.reason: Chinese former Hu viscount state does not mention the Huai; the marches clause is invented.

proposals.before: Feng, Zhuyi [22], Fuli, Zhujiu, the Xiao county on the Xiao River, Hong, and the Xiao seat farther east.
proposals.after: Feng, Zhuyi [22], Fuli, Zhujiu, Xiao, Hong, and Xiao counties.
proposals.reason: The source lists three county names after Zhujiu; the river gloss and duplicated Xiao seats are not in the Chinese.

proposals.before: 〈The Qufu basin where the Duke of Zhou's son Boqin ruled Lu.〉
proposals.after: 〈The Qufu basin where Lu Marquis Boqin dwelt.〉
proposals.reason: Chinese names only Lu Marquis Boqin at Qufu and does not call him the Duke of Zhou son.

proposals.before: When Huainan passed north, Danyang exiles papered Huainan commandery at Lake Yu.
proposals.after: When Huainan passed north, Danyang exiles papered Huainan commandery at Yuhu.
proposals.reason: 于湖 is the place-name Yuhu, not a lake called Yu; the literal field already has Yuhu.

proposals.before: Ningkang one shifted the provincial seat to Gushu.
proposals.after: In the first year of Ningkang, the garrison was moved to Gushu.
proposals.reason: Ningkang one is ungrammatical for 寧康元年; 移鎮 is moving the garrison or seat.

proposals.before: 〈Once the drum polity of the Gu viscounts.〉
proposals.after: 〈Once the state of the Gu viscount.〉
proposals.reason: 鼓子國 names the Gu viscount's state; rendering 鼓 as drum obscures the proper name already used in the literal field.

proposals.before: Liwei county.
proposals.after: Liwu county.
proposals.reason: 蠡吾 is Lǐwú; Liwei misreads 吾.

proposals.before: King Wu settled Yin and enfeoffed Duke Shao in Yan; afterward he and the six states alike styled themselves kings.
proposals.after: King Wu settled Yin and enfeoffed Duke Shao in Yan; afterward Yan and the six states alike styled themselves kings.
proposals.reason: 其後與六國俱稱王 refers to later Yan, not Duke Shao as 'he' into the Warring States.

proposals.before: Liu Shan of Shu raised this seat to a public dukedom.〉
proposals.after: Liu Shan, sovereign of Shu, was tied to this county as a ducal fief.〉
proposals.reason: Public dukedom mistranslates 縣公; the note records a county dukedom linked to Liu Shan.

proposals.before: After Emperor Hui, You Province submitted to Shi Le.
proposals.after: After Emperor Hui, You Province fell to Shi Le.
proposals.reason: 沒於 means the province fell into Shi Le's hands, not a voluntary submission.

proposals.before: After Jun fell, Murong Wei lost Former Yan to Fu Jian.
proposals.after: When Jun died, his son Murong Wei was destroyed by Fu Jian.
proposals.reason: 雋死 is Jun's death, 子 marks Murong Wei as his son, and 爲苻堅所滅 is destruction by Fu Jian.

proposals.before: Once Gongsun Wenyi fell, the Eastern Yi colonel alone remained at Xiangping.
proposals.after: After Wenyi was extinguished, there was a Protector-Colonel of the Eastern Yi at Xiangping.
proposals.reason: 滅後 is after Wenyi's destruction; 護東夷校尉 is the protector-colonel; alone is not in the Chinese.

proposals.before: Pingzhou's first inspector was Murong Hui, but Yongjia's chaos soon lifted him as chief protector.
proposals.after: When Pingzhou was first established, Murong Hui was made its inspector; then, amid the Yongjia turmoil, Hui was acclaimed by the multitude.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic rendering invents 'chief protector' and makes Yongjia 'lift' Hui; the Chinese says Hui was acclaimed by the multitude after being appointed inspector.

proposals.before: Murong Bao retreated to Helong, and Wei swallowed everything from Youzhou south to Lupu stockade.
proposals.after: Afterward Murong Chui's son Bao again moved to Helong; from Youzhou down to the land south of Lupu garrison fell into Wei hands.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic line drops Murong Chui as father and turns the second move into a retreat.

proposals.before: Murong Xi scattered his kinsmen as inspectors—Youzhou at Lingzhi, Qingzhou at Xincheng, Bingzhou at Fancheng, Yingzhou at Sujun, Jizhou at Feiru.
proposals.after: Murong Xi posted the Youzhou inspector at Lingzhi, the Qingzhou inspector at Xincheng, the Bingzhou inspector at Fancheng, the Yingzhou inspector at Sujun, and the Jizhou inspector at Feiru.
proposals.reason: The Chinese only stations inspectors at named garrisons; 'scattered his kinsmen' is not in the source.

proposals.before: Feng Ba seized the throne at Helong, kept the Yan dynastic name, and Wei eventually crushed him.
proposals.after: Later Feng Ba usurped him; Ba arrogated an imperial style at Helong, still reckoned as Later Yan, and finally fell to Wei.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic sentence omits the usurpation of Gao Yun and replaces the Later Yan identification with a looser paraphrase.

proposals.before: Yuanhai stationed Yongzhou at Pingyang and Youzhou at Lishi.
proposals.after: Yuanhai stationed the Yongzhou inspector at Pingyang and the Youzhou inspector at Lishi.
proposals.reason: The Chinese posts 雍州刺史 and 幽州刺史, the inspectors, not the provinces as such.

proposals.before: Shi Le pacified Shuofang and revived Shuozhou.
proposals.after: Shi Le pacified Shuofang and again established Shuozhou.
proposals.reason: 又置朔州 means he established Shuozhou again, not that he revived an existing one in the English sense.

proposals.before: Examining the Tribute of Yu, the land of the Black River and Western River—Shun established twelve herds; this is one of them.
proposals.after: Examining the Tribute of Yu, the land of the Black River and Western River—Shun established twelve pastors; this is one of them.
proposals.reason: 十二牧 are regional pastors, not herds of animals.

proposals.before: 〈Homeland of Duke Zheng, brother to King Xuan of Zhou.〉
proposals.after: 〈Town of Duke Huan of Zheng, younger brother of King Xuan of Zhou.〉
proposals.reason: 鄭桓公 is Duke Huan of Zheng; 弟 is younger brother; 邑 is his town.

proposals.before: 〈Earl Zheng of Zhou King Xuan's younger brother.〉
proposals.after: 〈The town of Duke Huan of Zheng, younger brother of King Xuan of Zhou.〉
proposals.reason: 桓公 is Duke Huan, and the English order obscures that he is King Xuan's younger brother whose town this was.

proposals.before: 〈Old Daliyang; Qin seized it and rechristened the seat.
proposals.after: 〈Formerly Dali; Qin seized it and renamed the seat.
proposals.reason: 大荔 is the Dali polity or people-name, not a toponym Daliyang; the English invents the -yang ending.

proposals.before: 〈Formerly Daliyang; Qin captured it and renamed.
proposals.after: 〈Formerly Dali; Qin captured it and renamed it.
proposals.reason: 大荔 should be Dali, not Daliyang.

proposals.before: 〈When Duke Wu of Qin smashed the Ji Rong he carved out this county; Shanggui already lay upstream, so the name was prefixed with "Lower."〉
proposals.after: 〈When Duke Wu of Qin smashed the Gui Rong he carved out this county; Shanggui already lay upstream, so the name was prefixed with "Lower."〉
proposals.reason: 邽戎 is Gui Rong; Ji is the wrong romanization of 邽.

proposals.before: 〈Duke Wu of Qin attacked the Ji Rong and set up the county; because there was already Shanggui, he prefixed 「lower」 to the name.〉
proposals.after: 〈Duke Wu of Qin attacked the Gui Rong and set up the county; because there was already Shanggui, he prefixed 「lower」 to the name.〉
proposals.reason: 邽戎 should be Gui Rong, not Ji Rong.

proposals.before: 〈Han raised it as chief ennoblements officer, then Right Fufeng under Taichu.
proposals.after: 〈Emperor Wu of Han made it the chief commandant of nobility, then renamed it Right Fufeng during Taichu.
proposals.reason: The Chinese subject is 漢武帝; the idiomatic English drops the emperor and softens 以為主爵都尉 / 更名.

proposals.before: 〈Yong paired with the marquis chancellor.
proposals.after: 〈A marquisate seat administered by a chancellor.
proposals.reason: 侯相 marks a county governed as a marquisate by a chancellor, not a pairing of Yong with a person.

proposals.before: 〈Marquis chancellor.
proposals.after: 〈Marquis-chancellor seat.
proposals.reason: 侯相 is the administrative status of the county, not a bare office title standing alone.

proposals.before: It shelters five suburban altars and more than three hundred shrines to Taihao, the Yellow Emperor, and their successors.〉
proposals.after: It has five suburban altars and three hundred three shrines from Taihao and the Yellow Emperor downward.〉
proposals.reason: 三百三所 is three hundred three precincts, not an indefinite more than three hundred.

proposals.before: 〈Archaic Hu fell when heir Qi struck north.〉
proposals.after: 〈An ancient state, attacked by Qi of Xia.〉
proposals.reason: 夏啟所伐 says Xia Qi attacked the ancient state; the English invents heirship, the state falling, and a northward strike.

proposals.before: Gloss [29]: post-Jianxing turmoil forfeited Yongzhou to Liu Cong.
proposals.after: After the Jianxing era, Yongzhou was lost to Liu Cong.
proposals.reason: The Chinese has no gloss label; 'Gloss [29]:' is an invented apparatus heading, and 'turmoil forfeited' is not in 建興之後，雍州沒於劉聰.

proposals.before: Once the Shi house fell, Fu Jian clamped Guanzhong and enthroned Former Qin at Chang'an.
proposals.after: Once the Shi house fell, Fu Jian (苻健) clamped Guanzhong and enthroned Former Qin at Chang'an.
proposals.reason: English 'Fu Jian' here renders 苻健, but the next sentence uses the same spelling for a different ruler, 苻堅; the Chinese names must be distinguished.

proposals.before: Emperor Kang ordered Yu Yi west as Jingzhou inspector with seat at Xiangyang.
proposals.after: In Emperor Kang's time, Yu Yi served as inspector of Jingzhou and moved his seat to Xiangyang.
proposals.reason: 康帝時 is a reign-time frame, not an order, and 遷鎮襄陽 is relocating the garrison to Xiangyang, not sending Yu Yi 'west'.

proposals.before: Qin-Yong exiles spilling through Fan and Mian persuaded Emperor Xiaowu to stage Yongzhou at Xiangyang plus seven attached commanderies.
proposals.after: After Qin-Yong exiles poured south through Fan and Mian, Emperor Xiaowu first established a provisional Yongzhou at Xiangyang together with seven attached commanderies.
proposals.reason: The Chinese 始於 states that Xiaowu first planted the provisional province; it does not say the refugees persuaded him.

proposals.before: Classical geography marks this as Yongzhou's western bound; Zhou's decay left it to Rong and Di bands.
proposals.after: By the Tribute of Yu this marked Yongzhou's western bound; when Zhou declined the land fell to the Di.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names only 狄; the idiomatic line invents Rong alongside Di.

proposals.before: Qin's Ganquan halls at Meiyang echoed the Xiongnu golden idols raised for Heaven.
proposals.after: Qin built the Ganquan palace at Meiyang, originally the place where the Xiongnu cast golden figures to sacrifice to Heaven.
proposals.reason: 本…之處 identifies the site of earlier Xiongnu Heaven sacrifice; 'echoed' invents a mere architectural resemblance.

proposals.before: Seven years later Qinzhou returned with seat at Shanggui.
proposals.after: In the seventh year it was restored, with its seat at Shanggui.
proposals.reason: Chinese 七年 continues Taikang from the previous sentence (Taikang 7), not an interval of seven years after Taikang 3.

proposals.before: Li Gao's Western Liang flew its banner from Dunhuang.
proposals.after: Prince Wuzhao's Western Liang flew its banner from Dunhuang.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names only 武昭王; Li Gao is not in this unit.

proposals.before: At Guzang Lü Guang listened to Guo Mo's omens and dubbed Changsong Eastern Zhangye.
proposals.after: At Guzang Lü Guang listened to Guo Nen's omens and dubbed Changsong Eastern Zhangye.
proposals.reason: 郭黁 is Nen/Nun (Nún), not Mo.

proposals.before: Emperor Hui stitched Didao Commandery from nine counties carved out of Longxi.
proposals.after: Emperor Hui split Didao, Lintao, and Heguan from Longxi, also established the six counties Taoyang, Suiping, Wujie, Shixing, Diwu, and Zhenqiu, and from those nine counties created Didao Commandery, attaching it to Qinzhou.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic line omits the named Longxi counties, the six newly founded counties, and Qinzhou affiliation that the Chinese and literal fields list.

proposals.before: Exiles dubbed Liang-within-Liangzhou Northern Qinzhou at Qianchi.
proposals.after: East of the Yangtze they split Liang into Qin, which sojourned in Liangzhou, and they further established Dichi as Northern Qinzhou.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic rendering fuses two steps and misreads 氐池 as Qianchi and 江左分梁爲秦 as a nickname.

proposals.before: South of the Yangtze courtiers split Liang into Qin, lodged it inside Liangzhou, and raised Qianchi as Northern Qinzhou.
proposals.after: South of the Yangtze courtiers split Liang into Qin, lodged it inside Liangzhou, and raised Dichi as Northern Qinzhou.
proposals.reason: 氐池 is Dichi, not Qianchi.

proposals.before: In Chuping 6 Linqing County joined Yongning Commandery, per gloss .
proposals.after: In Emperor Xian's sixth year of Chuping, Linjiang County was attached to Yongning Commandery.
proposals.reason: 臨江 is Linjiang, not Linqing; 獻帝 is omitted; 'per gloss' is not in the Chinese.

proposals.before: In Emperor Xian's sixth year of Chuping Linqing County joined Yongning Commandery.
proposals.after: In Emperor Xian's sixth year of Chuping Linjiang County joined Yongning Commandery.
proposals.reason: 臨江 is Linjiang, not Linqing.

proposals.before: Liu Zhang converted Yongning into Badong and peeled Baxia from Ba.
proposals.after: In Jian'an 6 Liu Zhang renamed Yongning to Badong Commandery and split Dianjiang from Ba Commandery to create Baxi Commandery.
proposals.reason: 巴西 is Baxi, not Baxia, and the idiomatic line drops Jian'an 6 and Dianjiang.

proposals.before: the third year of Taishi raised Liangzhou at Hanzhong, upgraded Hanshou to Jinshou, and spun Xindu from Guanghan.
